title: Worktrees, hooks, signing and large files
summary: The tools that make a professional's Git smoother and safer: several checkouts at once, automatic checks, verified commits, and binaries done right.

steps.title: Worktrees: two branches checked out at once
body: Mid-feature, you must review a PR or fix production. Instead of stashing, check out another branch **in another folder** that shares the same repository:
```text
git worktree add ../shop-hotfix main      # new folder with main checked out
cd ../shop-hotfix                          # fix, commit, push: same .git, same objects
git worktree list
git worktree remove ../shop-hotfix
Each worktree has its own working tree, index and HEAD; commits, branches and stashes are shared. A branch can be checked out in only one worktree at a time.
Your half-done feature stays exactly as it was: no stash, no rebuild.

steps.prompt: Why can't you `git switch feature` in a second worktree while `feature` is checked out in the first?
options: Both worktrees would move the same branch with every commit, and one working tree would silently go stale; Git forbids it
steps.explain: Use `git switch --detach feature` there if you only need to look, or create a new branch.

steps.title: Hooks: automatic checks
body: Hooks are scripts Git runs at certain moments, from `.git/hooks/` (or a folder set with `core.hooksPath`, which lets a team commit them):
| Hook | Runs | Typical use |
| `pre-commit` | before the commit is created | format check, lint, **secret scan** |
| `commit-msg` | after the message is written | enforce message format, ticket ids |
| `pre-push` | before pushing | run fast tests |

A hook that exits non-zero **aborts** the operation. `git commit --no-verify` skips client-side hooks, so hooks are a convenience, not a security boundary: anything that must hold is also enforced **server-side** in CI and branch protection.
For .NET teams, tools like Husky.Net install and share hooks; `dotnet format --verify-no-changes` is a common pre-commit.

steps.title: Signing commits
body: Anyone can write `user.name = "Your CEO"` in their config; commit authorship is just text. **Signing** proves a commit really came from a key you control:
```text
git config --global gpg.format ssh                     # sign with an SSH key (simplest)
git config --global user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
git config --global commit.gpgsign true                # sign every commit
git log --show-signature -1
git tag -s v1.4.0 -m "Release 1.4.0"                   # signed tag
Upload the same public key to GitHub/GitLab as a **signing key**, and commits show **Verified**. Many organisations require signed commits on protected branches.

steps.title: Large files and binaries
body: Git keeps **every version of every file forever**, and each clone downloads all of it. A 200 MB video committed ten times is 2 GB in every clone, even after you delete it.
- Keep build outputs, packages and datasets **out** of Git (`.gitignore`; use NuGet feeds, artifact storage).
- For binaries that truly belong with the code (design files, game assets), use **Git LFS**: the repo stores a small pointer file; the content lives on an LFS server and is downloaded on checkout.
```text
git lfs install
git lfs track "*.psd"           # writes a rule into .gitattributes; commit it
git add .gitattributes design.psd
For huge repos: `git clone --filter=blob:none` (partial clone: fetch file contents on demand) and `git sparse-checkout` (only some folders).

build.title: Pre-commit secret scanner
transform: // Your passing code from the code-dojo Git track.

prompt: Write `Scan(Dictionary<string, string> files)` for a `pre-commit` hook. It returns one finding per matching line, as `path:line: rule`, files sorted by path (ordinal), lines in order (1-based), rules in this order:
A line can produce several findings. Use `System.Text.RegularExpressions.Regex.IsMatch`.
solution: var rules = new (string Name, string Pattern)[]
foreach (var (path, content) in files.OrderBy(f => f.Key, StringComparer.Ordinal))
hints: Keep the rules in an array of `(Name, Pattern)` tuples so the order is fixed.
Split each file on `\n` and loop with an index for the line number.
Use verbatim strings (`@"..."`) for the regexes.
template: Dojo.Eq("finds the secrets", new List<string> { "appsettings.json:2: password", "deploy.sh:1: AWS access key", "id_rsa:1: private key" }, Scan(dojoFiles));
Dojo.Eq("clean code passes", new List<string>(), Scan(new() { ["a.cs"] = "var passwordLength = 12;" }));
